tagline: Marshes and a basalt rim on the desert road from Burns to Fields.
intro: High Desert Discovery crosses Harney County’s juniper and sagebrush country, skirting refuge marshes before following Catlow Rim toward Fields. From Frenchglen, the road crosses a low pass into Catlow Valley; the final leg climbs over Long Hollow Summit and descends into Pueblo Valley. ODOT presents this Oregon Scenic Byway as a gateway to Steens Mountain and the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, and recommends five to seven hours. Wright’s Point offers views north to the Blue Mountains and south to Steens Mountain, before the route reaches the Narrows.

The route began as a more expansive idea: in the early 1990s, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Land Management proposed a scenic byway between New Princeton and Lakeview. Their plan included three visitor centers and 24 interpretive waysides, but no national byway was established. Oregon designated the shorter High Desert Discovery route in 2003, without the proposed visitor centers.

Leave Burns on OR 78, then turn south onto OR 205 toward the Narrows between Harney and Malheur lakes. The drive follows the refuge to Frenchglen and its historic hotel, then continues into Catlow Valley. Follow the basalt rim south before the road turns toward Fields, the byway’s ranching-community endpoint.

moments.title: Narrows
moments.text: At the Narrows interpretive site, Mud Lake and Harney Lake lie to the west, with Malheur Lake and the wildlife refuge to the east. The settlement began in 1889, when Lewis B. Springer and Albert Hembree established a community. Springer named the post office after himself; in 1892 it became Narrows, and Hembree took over as postmaster. The post office operated until 1936. The interpretive site sits near the bridge between Harney and Malheur lakes, on the byway’s crossing of the Harney Basin. The neighboring refuge supports 320 bird species, with migrations in spring and fall.
moments.notice: The interpretive site offers views west toward Mud Lake and Harney Lake.

moments.title: Frenchglen Hotel
moments.text: The Frenchglen Hotel’s early guests included people doing business at Peter French’s P Ranch and visitors to the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge. Schoolteachers stayed here too. Civilian Conservation Corps labor helped restore and enlarge the hotel in 1937 and 1938. The Oregon Parks and Recreation Department took possession in 1973; the property entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. The historic building contains eight guest rooms, distinct from the modern Drovers’ Inn used for overflow guests. The American Foursquare building stands near the base of Steens Mountain, at the northern end of its loop road.

moments.title: Catlow Rim
moments.text: Catlow Rim grows from rolling hills at the valley’s north end into a cliff more than 1,000 feet above the floor at its southern end. The basalt escarpment is the western face of the Steens Mountain fault block, along the valley’s eastern side. The valley itself is a graben, a tectonic depression between the uplifted fault blocks of Hart Mountain and Steens Mountain. During the Pleistocene, a large lake covered the valley. Shoreline erosion marks, gravel bars and terraces cut by waves remain as evidence, especially at the rim’s base. The road parallels this rim before turning east toward Fields.
moments.notice: The rim becomes steeper and higher toward the southern end of Catlow Valley.
